subject: frontend-engineering
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (The Time × Place Grid, Trade-off Profile, When to Choose Each Model, Hydration, Edge Rendering, Partial Prerendering, Verification, Do NOT Use When) and current web rendering practice (web.dev Rendering on the Web, React Server Components, Core Web Vitals).

cases.scenario: A marketing site renders every route with SSR (the framework default). Pages never change between deploys and carry no personalization, yet the team pays request-time render cost on every visit and TTFB spikes under traffic.
cases.context: Content is fully static and updated only on deploy. The team wants lower cost and faster first paint without losing crawlability.
cases.question: How should the agent change the rendering strategy for these routes?
expected_flags: Identifies these routes' content profile as static (no per-request data, no personalization)
Recommends SSG (build-time, CDN-cached) instead of SSR for static marketing routes
Notes SSG gives best FCP/LCP and lowest request-time server cost while staying crawlable
Frames model choice as per-route, not a single app-wide default
expected_fix_hints: Move static routes to build-time generation (SSG); use ISR/on-demand revalidation only if content updates between deploys
Reserve SSR for routes that actually need per-request data
absent_signals: Do not keep SSR for fully static content just because it is the framework default
Do not switch the static pages to CSR (loses fast first paint and crawl reliability)

cases.scenario: A dashboard is server-rendered and Lighthouse shows a good FCP, but real users report the page is unresponsive for seconds after it appears: buttons do nothing and inputs lag. The client JS bundle is ~1.8MB.
cases.context: The team concluded that because FCP is good, rendering is 'solved' and the slowness must be a backend issue.
cases.question: What should the agent diagnose and recommend?
expected_flags: Identifies hydration cost, not HTML production, as the bottleneck (TTI/INP, not FCP)
States HTML production speed and hydration cost are independent — a fast-SSR page with a large bundle is not interactive until JS loads/parses/executes
Recommends reducing what hydrates: RSC (server components excluded from the client bundle), islands, or progressive hydration
Points to measuring TTI/INP in real-user conditions, not lab FCP
expected_fix_hints: Convert non-interactive subtrees to Server Components so they ship no client JS
Code-split and shrink the client bundle; hydrate interactive islands only
absent_signals: Do not conclude the page is fast because FCP is good
Do not treat hydration cost as a backend/server-render problem

cases.scenario: A product-detail route has a large static layout (description, specs, images) plus a small per-user 'recommended for you' block and a live stock indicator. Today it is fully SSR so the whole page waits on the slow recommendation service before any paint.
cases.context: Most of the page could be cached; only two small regions are dynamic/personalized. The team wants instant first paint without removing the dynamic blocks.
cases.question: Which rendering model fits, and how should the page be staged?
expected_flags: Recommends PPR: static shell at build time + streamed dynamic holes (recommendations, stock) at request time
Notes the user sees the cached shell instantly while the dynamic regions stream in
Considers ISR for the catalog portion if it updates periodically; SSR only if the dynamic part dominates
Reasons from the mixed content profile rather than forcing one model for the whole route
expected_fix_hints: Adopt partial prerendering (or streaming SSR + CDN-cached shell) so the slow region does not block first paint
Cache the static portion and isolate the personalized blocks as streamed/dynamic
absent_signals: Do not keep the whole route blocking on the slowest dynamic region
Do not make the whole route fully static (would drop personalization and live stock)

cases.scenario: A team moves a per-request route to edge SSR for lower TTFB to a global audience. The route opens a direct TCP database connection during render, and it fails or times out at the edge.
cases.context: The audience is geographically distributed and the route genuinely needs per-request rendering.
cases.question: What is wrong, and how should the agent reconcile edge rendering with the data layer?
expected_flags: Identifies that edge runtimes are constrained (Web Standard APIs, typically no direct DB connections)
Confirms edge SSR is appropriate for a global, per-request route — the rendering placement is fine
The fix is the data access path, not abandoning edge
Recommends HTTP-accessible data (origin API or data proxy), or a hybrid: edge for render, origin for data
expected_fix_hints: Access data over HTTP from the edge (origin API / data gateway) instead of a direct DB connection
Use a hybrid: render at the edge, fetch from origin; prefer cacheable fetches to avoid a round-trip per request
absent_signals: Do not blame edge rendering itself and revert without addressing data access
Do not assume full Node.js APIs (including direct DB drivers) are available at the edge

cases.scenario: An architect proposes a single rule for the whole app: 'logged-out pages CSR, logged-in pages SSR.' The app has a static docs section, a per-query search page, a real-time chart, and an admin panel hit weekly.
cases.context: The team is treating the decision as SSR-vs-CSR and applying it by login state rather than per-route content profile.
cases.question: How should the agent respond to the proposed rule?
expected_flags: Flags SSR-vs-CSR as a false binary; the space is 6-8 models on a time × place grid
Maps each route to a fitting model: docs → SSG (+ client search); search → SSR/streaming SSR; real-time chart → CSR/RSC + client island; admin → RSC or SSR
Rejects login-state as the discriminator; the discriminator is content profile (static/dynamic/personalized) and performance constraints
Keeps the decision per-route, validated by measurement
expected_fix_hints: Replace the blanket rule with a per-route mapping from content profile to model
Use SSG for static docs, streaming SSR for slow search, RSC/CSR island for the chart
absent_signals: Do not adopt a single app-wide SSR/CSR rule
Do not pick the model from login state instead of content profile

cases.scenario: A PM asks the rendering-models owner to (a) reorganize the frontend folder structure into feature modules and (b) design the HTTP Cache-Control headers and CDN purge strategy for the API responses.
cases.context: The team conflates 'rendering' with all frontend and delivery decisions.
cases.question: How should the agent scope the request?
expected_flags: Folder/module reorganization is out of scope — that is frontend-architecture
Cache-Control headers / CDN purge / content negotiation is out of scope — that is http-semantics (the wire protocol)
Offers the in-scope adjacency: which rendering model each route should use, which then informs (but does not own) caching
Correctly redirects rather than answering out of lane
expected_fix_hints: Route codebase organization to frontend-architecture and HTTP caching to http-semantics
Provide the per-route model choices that those skills can build on
absent_signals: Do not design the folder structure
Do not author the HTTP cache headers / purge policy

cases.scenario: A blog uses SSG with a time-based revalidation (ISR) window of 24 hours. Editors publish a correction and expect it live immediately, but readers see the old post for hours.
cases.context: The team wants fast cached delivery for normal traffic but immediate freshness when an editor publishes.
cases.question: How should the agent reconcile cached delivery with on-publish freshness?
expected_flags: Recognizes the route correctly uses a build-time model (SSG/ISR) for a mostly-static blog
Flags the time-based-only revalidation as the cause of the stale window
Recommends on-demand revalidation triggered by the publish event (not just a TTL)
Notes SSG/ISR caches must be validated to invalidate correctly on content updates
expected_fix_hints: Add on-demand revalidation on publish so corrections go live immediately
Keep the TTL as a backstop, but drive freshness from the publish action
absent_signals: Do not switch the whole blog to SSR just to get freshness
Do not rely solely on the 24h TTL for editor-published corrections
